Analyse a published administrative table in one call

Source: R/analyse_table.R
analyse_table.Rd

The questions asked of a published table are always the same: what is in it, what changed between periods and how sure can one be, what the rates are if there is an exposure, whether a short series trends, and whether this release differs from the one held before. Each has a function in this package; this runs them together, with the pieces a reviewer needs and that are easy to forget on a deadline: exact intervals on every change, multiple-comparison adjustment over the groups scanned, the envelope that rounding and suppression in the release imply, and a drift screen against the prior capsule.

Usage

analyse_table(
  data,
  value,
  period,
  by = NULL,
  population = NULL,
  prior = NULL,
  units = c("count", "continuous", "percent"),
  rounding = NULL,
  rounding_kind = c("nearest", "random"),
  suppression_limit = NULL,
  direction = c("neutral", "higher_is_better", "lower_is_better"),
  per = 1000,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  alpha = 0.05,
  adjust = "BH"
)

Arguments

data

A data frame in long form: one row per period and group.

value

Name of the column (a string) with the published count (or measure).

period

Name of the column with the period (fiscal year, quarter, ...); numeric periods are used as the time axis of the trend tests.

by

Optional character vector of grouping column names (institution, region, ...). NULL (the default) treats the table as one series.

population

Optional name of an exposure column for rates (NULL, the default, skips the rate step).

prior

Optional data frame: the previous capsule of the same table, for the drift screen. NULL (the default) skips it.

units

"count" (the default), "continuous" or "percent", as in yoy().

rounding, rounding_kind, suppression_limit

How the release rounds or suppresses cells; see published_bounds(). rounding is the rounding base (for example 5), rounding_kind "nearest" (the default) or "random", suppression_limit the threshold below which cells are suppressed. NULL when the counts are exact. Used only for counts: with other units they are ignored, with a warning.

direction

Which way is an improvement, as in yoy(): "neutral" (the default), "higher_is_better" or "lower_is_better".

per

Rate denominator, as in rate(); default 1000 (rates per 1,000 of population).

conf_level

Confidence level for every interval, default 0.95.

alpha

Level for the multiple-comparison decision and the drift screens, default 0.05.

adjust

Multiple-comparison method for scan_adjust(), default "BH" (Benjamini-Hochberg).

Value

A list of class bricklayer_analysis (with a print method that summarises it in a few lines):

profile

profile_columns() of data.

missingness

named numeric from missingness_summary().

change

the yoy() table; for counts with the added columns p_value, p_adjusted and significant, and with env_* and combined_pct_lower/combined_pct_upper when publication bounds were requested.

rates, rate_change

the rate() and rate_change() tables when population is given, otherwise NULL.

trend

data frame with one row per group: the by columns, periods, first, last, tau, trend_p, slope, rate_ratio, rate_ratio_lower, rate_ratio_upper.

drift

capsule_drift() result against prior, or NULL.

meta

list of the arguments used, n_rows, the sorted periods, prior (logical) and when (a time stamp).

Details

The steps, in order:

  1. profile: profile_columns() and missingness_summary() on data;

  2. change: yoy() between consecutive periods within each by group. For units = "count" the exact p-values are then adjusted across all comparisons with scan_adjust(), and, when rounding or suppression_limit is given, yoy_bounds() adds the publication envelope (see published_bounds()). For "continuous" and "percent" units neither step runs: rounding and suppression_limit are then ignored, with a warning;

  3. rates (only with population): rate() per group and period, and rate_change() between periods, adjusted with scan_adjust();

  4. trend: per group, the values summed within each period, then trend_test() (Mann-Kendall tau, p-value and Theil-Sen slope) and, for counts, count_trend() (Poisson rate ratio per period). A group with fewer than three periods gets NA; a test that fails gets NA rather than an error;

  5. drift (only with prior): capsule_drift() of data against prior.

Nothing is written and nothing is fetched; a progress bar for the trend step is drawn on stderr unless options(morie.quiet = TRUE). Errors: data or prior not a data frame; a named column not in data; an invalid units, direction or rounding_kind; a conf_level outside (0, 1); and any error of the functions called (for example negative counts in yoy()).

See also

report_analysis() writes the result as a Markdown or HTML report.

Examples

path <- system.file("extdata", "otis_a01_individuals.csv",
                    package = "rmoriebricklayer")
otis <- read.csv(path)
a <- analyse_table(otis, value = "individuals", period = "year",
                   by = c("table", "group"))
a
#> Analysis of `individuals` by year over 3 period(s) (2023 to 2025), grouped by table x group
#>   rows 15, columns 4; no missing values
#>   change: 10 comparison(s), 9 significant after BH at 0.05
#>   trend: 0 of 5 series with Mann-Kendall p < 0.05
a$change[, c("table", "group", "year", "pct_change", "p_adjusted")]
#> <rmbl_yoy: no periods>
a$trend[, c("group", "tau", "trend_p", "rate_ratio")]
#>      group       tau   trend_p rate_ratio
#> 1 18 to 24 0.3333333 1.0000000   1.027143
#> 2 25 to 49 0.3333333 1.0000000   1.118024
#> 3      50+ 0.3333333 1.0000000   1.112728
#> 4   Female 1.0000000 0.3333333   1.376319
#> 5     Male 0.3333333 1.0000000   1.077781

# counts published rounded to base 5: the intervals widen
b <- analyse_table(otis, value = "individuals", period = "year",
                   by = c("table", "group"), rounding = 5)
b$change[1:3, c("group", "year", "pct_lower", "combined_pct_lower")]
#> <rmbl_yoy: no periods>

# rates with an exposure column
d <- data.frame(year = rep(2019:2022, 2), site = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 4),
                n = c(10, 12, 15, 9, 30, 28, 35, 40),
                pop = rep(c(1000, 2000), each = 4))
r <- analyse_table(d, "n", "year", by = "site", population = "pop", per = 1000)
r$rate_change[, c("site", "year", "rate", "rate_ratio", "p_adjusted")]
#> ──  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 
#>  site year rate rate_ratio p_adjusted
#>     A 2019 10.0         NA         NA
#>     A 2020 12.0  1.2000000  0.8956832
#>     A 2021 15.0  1.2500000  0.8956832
#>     A 2022  9.0  0.6000000  0.8956832
#>     B 2019 15.0         NA         NA
#>     B 2020 14.0  0.9333333  0.8956832
#>     B 2021 17.5  1.2500000  0.8956832
#>     B 2022 20.0  1.1428571  0.8956832
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── 

# a column that is not in the data is an error
try(analyse_table(otis, value = "count", period = "year"))
#> Error : column `count` not found in `data`
